oil.summary: A sharp divergence dominated the crude complex today: WTI held near flat (+0.36% to $92.73) while Brent cratered 6% to $98.06, compressing the Brent-WTI spread dramatically. Products were hit harder still, with RBOB off 6.76% and heating oil down 3.36%, suggesting demand-side concerns are cutting through the geopolitical premium. The backdrop remains acutely uncertain: Iran's 7-day Hormuz reopening plan has reportedly been rejected by Trump, Saudi Arabia's foreign minister is in Washington for emergency talks, and Ukraine struck Russian oil facilities overnight. Offsetting some upside pressure, the U.S. SPR hit its lowest level since 1982 at 284.6 million barrels. Russia's new decree blacking out export and refinery data further clouds supply visibility. CME options imply a 77% probability of an OPEC cut at the next meeting, reflecting market anxiety about demand.
drivers: Brent -6% on reports Trump rejected Iran's Hormuz reopening plan, injecting fresh ceasefire uncertainty into the market
U.S. SPR falls to a 44-year low of 284.6 mb, limiting the government's buffer against supply shocks
Russia imposes new secrecy decree on energy export data, compounding supply-side opacity as Ukraine strikes Russian oil facilities

gas.summary: Natural gas prices pulled back modestly on the day — Henry Hub -1.81% to $3.138/MMBtu and TTF -1.33% to €71.11/MWh — but both benchmarks remain well up on the month. The session's dominant structural story is QatarEnergy extending its LNG force majeure through end-November as Hormuz traffic remains constrained, effectively keeping a floor under European prices. High freight costs are diverting U.S. LNG cargoes toward Europe rather than Asia, providing some relief to European buyers while tightening the Atlantic basin. An Asian switch from gas to coal — partly responsible for Indonesia's coal exports falling 23% — is paradoxically tightening coal markets globally. Today's mild price decline looks corrective rather than trend-reversing given the persistent supply constraints.
drivers: QatarEnergy extends LNG force majeure through end-November, keeping structural supply tightness in place for European and Asian buyers
High freight costs close the U.S.-Asia LNG arbitrage, redirecting more U.S. LNG to Europe and capping near-term European upside
Asian gas-to-coal switching tightens thermal coal markets but reduces near-term gas demand pressure in the region

power.summary: Power and carbon markets were relatively quiet on price action today — EU EUAs slipped 0.84% to $81.93, holding within recent ranges and up ~5% on the month. The most notable headline was the UK National Energy System Operator flagging a 1.4 GW margin shortfall for Monday evening, a precautionary warning that underscores how thin reserve margins can become as the heating season approaches. The Trump-Xi summit delivered only a two-month trade truce extension, which markets received coolly and which offers little near-term relief to energy demand or supply-chain dynamics. Indonesia's coal export decline — driven by Asian buyers switching to coal from gas amid the Hormuz crisis — points to tightening traded coal availability that could eventually feed through to European power prices. Data for this sector was relatively limited today.
drivers: UK grid operator warns of a 1.4 GW margin shortfall Monday evening, highlighting thin reserve buffers heading into autumn
EU EUAs stable near $81.93, consolidating a ~5% monthly gain with no major fundamental catalyst to break the range today
Trump-Xi trade truce extension left flat by markets; no demand-side relief anticipated for near-term power or carbon fundamentals
